claims.text: An integrated experimental–simulation approach can separately quantify lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to earlier models.
The relevant samples are pristine homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr and a variant containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Full anharmonic DFT-based phonon Boltzmann calculations can provide the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution for this alloy.
TDTR can explicitly resolve the lattice contribution while Hall measurements resolve the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
The proposed measurements and simulations apply over 200–1200 K.
Pristine samples isolate intrinsic lattice transport at low temperature.
A 1 wt.% oxygen specimen mimics realistic defect-induced scattering at high temperatures.
Atomic-scale defects and microstructural disorder will be incorporated into the DFT simulations.
Separating anharmonic lattice transport from experimentally measured electronic transport avoids Debye-model and defect-free-crystal oversimplifications.
Resolving the two carrier contributions enables simulation parameters to be tuned to observed scattering mechanisms and microstructural complexity.
The combined prediction will have 20–30% lower uncertainty than previous predictions.
Below 200 K, lattice thermal conductivity will dominate electronic thermal conductivity.
From 300 to 1200 K, the electronic contribution will become comparable to or greater than the lattice contribution.
The predicted total conductivity for oxygen-containing specimens should match or improve upon observed values of 10–17 W/(K m).
Earlier approaches used ideal defect-free crystals and Debye approximations that conflated lattice and electronic contributions.
The cited PbSnTeSe work presents a complete HEA transport workflow using SQS, DFT, Boltzmann transport, and Green–Kubo methods.
The PbSnTeSe workflow is an adequate analogue supporting the proposed accuracy improvement in HfNbTaTiZr.
Unaccounted defect states or interfacial phenomena could alter the magnitude of the predicted improvement.
A deviation greater than 20–30% from measured total conductivity, or failure to observe low-temperature lattice dominance, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experimental range is defined as 200–1200 K, but the prediction and falsification rule require determining transport dominance below 200 K, which the stated experiment cannot test.
The hypothesis predicts lattice dominance below 200 K, whereas the task states that experiments below 200 K found lattice and electronic contributions to be comparable.

The 20–30% quantity is variously defined as a relative improvement in accuracy, a reduction in uncertainty, and an allowed absolute prediction error. These are different metrics, so the success and falsification criteria are not aligned.
